After a boy in their neighborhood fell into a septic tank, Kevin installed a scanner on his dashboard; he believed he could have helped if he’d heard the call. He’d listen to emergency dispatches while driving home from Little League and say, “We’re close by. Let’s just go check it out.” Kevin would pull over if he saw a car accident and extricate someone from the wreck before EMS arrived. He’d tell his sons not to be bystanders. “Don’t sit on the sidelines. Make things happen. Do things.” Once, when Kevin saw smoke coming from a building in their neighborhood, he told the boys to call the fire department and then ran off, grabbed a garden hose, and climbed through a back window to start putting the blaze out himself. He was strict and exacting with his sons. For every minute they were late to something, Kevin docked them half an hour of free time. When they were old enough, he enlisted them in construction work, and didn’t pay them until they could lift heavy loads. “You work like a man, you get paid like a man.” He once called James home from a friend’s house because he hadn’t cleaned his room. He marched James into the doorway and said, “Look at that.” There was a pair of socks on the floor. Patrick was growing into a burly achiever who aspired to West Point. James was slighter, milder, but with a distance runner’s stamina. During long car rides in New York gridlock, Kevin would ask the boys what they intended to do with their lives. Their grandfather was a butcher. Their father was a fireman. “I want you to be the next step up from that,” Kevin told them. “I want you to do something better than me.” By late summer 2001, Kevin had earned 20 citations for outstanding performance. He was beginning to think about retirement, and he dreamed of traveling—to Iceland in particular, with its volcanic landscape forged in fire. And the boys were nearly men. Patrick was 18 and had just started at Iona University, in New Rochelle, having been wait-listed at West Point. James was turning 17 and starting his senior year at Xavier High School in Manhattan. He wanted to be a firefighter. “You’re going to college,” Kevin insisted, but he took James on a scuba-training run under the Throgs Neck Bridge. James donned an FDNY dry suit and plunged into the dark, roiling East River while his father supervised from the boat. After the dive, someone took a picture of the two: Kevin’s hand is clapped on his son’s shoulder, and James, shrugging off the suit, is grinning widely. On Sunday, September 9, the family celebrated James’s birthday. Kevin had the day off and Patrick came down from Iona, and they barbecued and ate cake. Kevin and Patrick cloistered themselves in the den to work on his reapplication to West Point. Then Kevin drove Patrick back to school and kissed him on the cheek. “Love you. See you soon. I’ll talk to you next week.” Kevin reported to Rescue 4 at 6 p.m. on the evening of September 10 for a 24-hour shift. Liam Flaherty went off duty and headed to band practice at the Elks Lodge. Billy Murphy was on vacation. The kitchen was quiet. At 8:46 the next morning, American Airlines Flight 11 made a terrifying yeering sound as it accelerated into the North Tower of the World Trade Center. Rescue 4’s summons came at 8:55. Seven men hopped on the rig with Kevin: Terrence Farrell, William Mahoney, Peter Nelson, Durrell Pearsall, Peter Brennan, Allan Tarasiewicz, and a potential recruit named Michael Cawley. The ride probably took about 20 minutes. As they barreled toward Lower Manhattan, an unnerving alert came over the dispatch radio : “Be advised we have jumpers.” From a distance, Rescue 4 would have seen the smoke surging from floors 93 to 99 of the North Tower, the tallest building in New York. About seven minutes into their drive, they might have seen the blooming explosion of the second jet, United Airlines Flight 175, as it tilted into the South Tower between floors 77 and 85. Rescue 4 arrived at a scene that was too much for the senses. A torrent of debris fell from the buildings—shredded metal and insulation, chunks of concrete, shivering glass shards—amid an earsplitting clamor of sirens and screaming. Torsos, luggage, and aluminum scraps of 767s were strewn on the sidewalks. What looked like splashes of red paint on the plazas were the remains of jumpers who had pinwheeled from the upper floors of the North Tower. Kevin ran into a stunned fellow lieutenant named Robert LaRocco, from Ladder 9, who had seen a severed forearm with a perfectly manicured hand. LaRocco managed to get a call through to his wife. He told her, “It’s raining people.” Kevin reported to a command post across the street from the North Tower, where the FDNY’s chief of special operations command, Ray Downey, was doling out orders. He assigned Rescue 4 to help with evacuations in the South Tower and, if possible, to get upstairs and beat back the fire. Kevin was seen lining up his men and talking to them intently. He then led them single file toward the South Tower, hugging the sides of buildings. A rescue squad would have had its hands full in the lobby alone. Elevators were broken, stairwells smoked, and radios were unreliable. People were streaming down, badly burned or bloody, and some had to be carried. One elevator had stopped just short of the ground floor with people trapped inside. Firefighters pried open the outer doors and could see their legs, but couldn’t find a way to lower the car enough to free them. Flaming jet fuel cascaded down the shaft as the crews worked. At 9:52 a.m., about half an hour after Kevin had arrived, a battalion chief named Orio Palmer reached the South Tower’s 78th floor, where the jet’s wing had inflicted mass casualties. “We’re going to need two engines up here,” Palmer radioed down. Wherever Kevin was—trying to force open elevators, or starting the slow ascent to 78—the elements of the fire were taking over. The second plane had struck the South Tower at more than 500 miles an hour, stripping the fireproofing from steel trusses and columns. The inferno fed on carpets, curtains, chairs, desks, computers. Plumes of soot trapped the heat. The temperature hit 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit , softening the bones of the building. At 9:59 a.m., the top of the South Tower sagged. Then it began to collapse. Beams and struts slammed into one another. As each floor failed, the falling mass increased, picking up velocity. About 500,000 tons of concrete and steel sped to the earth, reaching an estimated 124 miles an hour. Thomas Nilsson / Getty The South Tower collapses at 9:59 a.m., September 11, 2001. Lieutenant LaRocco of Ladder 9 had just put his foot on a stalled escalator on the north end of the South Tower’s mezzanine when he felt something like a wave in the floor. He heard a mounting roar, like a space shuttle taking off. The light in the windows vanished, as if someone had yanked a giant shade down. Kevin would have had little time to think about the sound above him. It took just 10 seconds for the tower to fall. As the mass neared the ground, it generated a huge blast of compressed air and seismic waves equal to those produced by a 2.1-magnitude earthquake. Paperwork from the towers drifted miles away, littering the beaches of the Rockaways. For most of that day, RoseEllen had been at P.S. 312, preoccupied with getting her third graders back to their parents. Now, at home, she waited for Kevin to call. He always did, leaving a message when she didn’t answer. “Hey, it’s me. If you see anything on the news, don’t worry about it. I’m okay.” But 6 p.m. came and went without any word. At 12:30 a.m., Special Operations Command called and told RoseEllen that Kevin was listed among the missing; all of the guys on Rescue 4’s rig were unaccounted for, as was their captain, Brian Hickey, who had been working with Rescue 3 that day. RoseEllen stayed up all night, her eyes darting between the television news and the front door. Around sunrise, RoseEllen went onto the porch and stared down the street. “At that point, I knew,” she would say, years later. “In my head, I knew.” After a week, one of the crews digging through the pulverized wreckage at Ground Zero came across a Halligan bar, which might have been used to claw at an elevator door. It was marked with KD and R4 . Kevin Dowdell, Rescue 4 . The tool had been blown out of the lobby. But there was no other sign of Kevin. Haruka Sakaguchi for The Atlantic James holds his father’s Halligan bar. The remaining men of Rescue 4 set up a war room in the firehouse, manned round-the-clock shifts to dig through the wreckage, and assigned a firefighter to liaise with each family who was missing someone. “Did we find him today?” RoseEllen would ask. No, Billy Murphy would say, day after day. Whenever the door to the Dowdell house opened, three faces would swivel toward it with hope. “We were like, ‘If anyone got out of there or could get out of there, it’s him,’ ” Patrick recalled, but it was always a relative or neighbor. Two weeks after the attacks, RoseEllen decided that sitting around the house in their grief was not doing them any good. “Listen,” she said to the boys. “You’re going back to school, and I’m going back to work.” On the drive to Iona, she persuaded Patrick to finish his reapplication to West Point. “You will not—we will not—use anything as an excuse in your life,” she said. Xavier High School was steeped in mourning; 60 alumni and close relatives of students and staff were lost. Counselors and priests watched James for signs of depression, but when RoseEllen pushed him to see a therapist, he protested. “All I do is talk to people,” he told her. He would channel his emotions into running, sometimes 12 miles at a time. Back at Iona, Patrick couldn’t concentrate. He called James and suggested that they go to Ground Zero to search for their father’s remains. “If we find him, I want to be there,” Patrick told James. “I want to see him. I want to help carry him out.” James heard his father’s voice in his head. Don’t sit on the sidelines. Make things happen. Do things. “I’ll meet you there,” James told his brother. Rescue 4 held a meeting about whether to allow them to join the search. They took a vote, and the boys won. Murphy and Flaherty geared them up with fire boots, gloves, Carhartt suits, helmets, and tools. The guys worried about giving the boys nightmares. Murphy warned them: “If we come across somebody, I’ll ask you to step away until we find out who it is.” The pile, as it was called, was eight stories of contorted metal, sticking up like giant fork tines, spread over 16 smoldering acres. The burning electrical smell was sickening. As Patrick and James clambered through it, they could feel heat in their boot soles. Grapplers lifted steel from the smoking heaps, and the diggers showed the boys what to look for underneath: a boot, a piece of helmet, the reflective tape from a turnout coat. But the main sign of human remains was the odor of decay. As soon as the diggers smelled it, they would wave at the machines to stop. The first time the boys were present for a recovery, the crew cast sidelong looks at James and Patrick. The men and boys removed their helmets. A chaplain was called. They stood at attention as the remains were carried away on a flag-draped stretcher. “You good?” Murphy asked Patrick. “Yeah, I’m good,” Patrick said. For seven months, James and Patrick worked at Ground Zero as much as they could. “Being away from it became harder than being there,” Patrick recalled. When his classes at Iona were done for the day, he’d find a ride to the city and dig half the night, then return to campus at 3 or 4 a.m. slit-eyed from ash and lack of sleep, stowing his dusty gear in a garbage bag in his dorm. James kept his Carhartts and tools in his Xavier locker. He would shed his school uniform—blue oxford shirt, necktie, insignia-patched sweater—and tromp out the schoolhouse door, transformed, in coveralls and boots. The crew found parts of helmets, and parts of people. They found impaled bodies that had to be cut away from the steel with torches. They found intact bodies in strange voids; how long had some people survived under the wreckage? Sometimes the boys just put bone fragments in buckets. Haruka Sakaguchi for The Atlantic . Courtesy of the Dowdell family. Top : Patrick, Liam Flaherty, and James at the St. Patrick’s Day parade in 1996. Middle : Patrick ( left ) and Flaherty at Ground Zero in spring 2002. Bottom : Rescue 4’s rig at Kevin’s memorial service in April 2002. At the firehouse, Patrick and James sat around the kitchen table debriefing like members of the company. They listened to the men of Rescue 4 wrestle with survivor’s guilt. If they had been on duty, they’d have been in the South Tower at 9:59 a.m. Survival was a matter of lefts and rights, as Flaherty said. They posed terrible “What if?” questions. Should the fire commanders have foreseen the towers’ collapse? If so, should they have kept men from going up? “Well, what was the alternative?” Flaherty argued at the table. “There’s people trapped upstairs. We have to go get them.” Could you imagine, he said, if the FDNY had just given up on the towers? “That would have been the worst day in the history of the fire department the other way.” The kitchen conversations were a kind of counseling for the boys. “We had our people, and we just talked amongst ourselves, and that was enough,” Patrick remembered. So were the funerals for firefighters they played at with the Emerald Society Pipes and Drums. They stood by graves in kilts and red tunics that Flaherty had given them, and performed “Amazing Grace” and “Going Home.” Many children of the dead were preschoolers or grade-schoolers. RoseEllen saw that the firefighters were helping to steady her sons. “Is school good?” Flaherty and others would ask the boys while they dug through the pile. “If your grades aren’t good, you can’t be here.” As a picture of Kevin’s movements with Rescue 4 emerged from survivor accounts, the recovery concentrated on a spot near the South Tower elevator shafts. In late October, on a day the boys were not working, a crew found the remains of four men from Rescue 4. But not Kevin’s. A few feet away was a large, burned-out space where fires had raged below the tonnage for weeks. “You recover two guys that were kind of close by to each other in the rubble, and then you don’t get anybody else,” Patrick said. “It’s really hard. You don’t know how that happens, but that’s how it happens.” On the morning of November 12, 2001, when an American Airlines plane accidentally crashed into the Rockaways shortly after takeoff, RoseEllen could see the smoke from the porch. “You are not going over there,” she told James. When Rescue 4 pulled up to the crash site, James was already there in his gear, hosing down a burning house. “You’re one of us now,” a firefighter told him. James, though just 17, took the FDNY entrance exam and passed. By spring, the pile had become a pit, with almost 1.8 million tons of debris removed. The site was practically broom-clean. The recovery process was down to DNA testing of the smallest fragments. Even then, no Kevin. “There’s nothing there,” Murphy told RoseEllen. “It’s over.” “Nothing?” she asked. “Nothing,” he said. They held Kevin’s memorial service on April 20, 2002. His casket was filled with dust from the spot where they believed he had died, and mementos of him: his extra turnout gear, a pair of fire boots, a copy of the Irish Voice newspaper, travel brochures for Iceland. Letters from his sons and siblings. Hundreds of people attended, including the mayor. Patrick played a bagpipe solo of “Amazing Grace” as the casket was carried into the church. “He was a teacher, mentor, tradesman, listener, and my best friend,” Patrick said during his eulogy, concluding with an Irish blessing that Kevin had recited to him: “May the best days of your past be the worst of your future.” The memorial service marked an abrupt end to months of mission. “It was so consuming from September to April that after it was all said and done, there was a sense of ‘Now what do we do?’ ” James recalled. Kevin was irrecoverable. But they had his voice. Don’t sit on the sidelines. Patrick had just been accepted to West Point, and in June he entered “Beast Barracks,” the academy’s rigorous six-week cadet-induction program. It made the news: 9/11 firefighter’s kid joins the War on Terror . Overnight, he went from friends consoling him to officers barking orders. He marched to breakfast, marched to lunch, and spent nights shining his shoes. What if he couldn’t cut it? He feared letting his father down. He refused to buy his mother a West Point sweatshirt. “I didn’t want it to be a constant reminder of my failure if I didn’t make it through,” Patrick said. The combination of mourning, loneliness, and self-doubt made him mutinous. He racked up punishment tours for lateness and absences, and was made to march in circles carrying a rifle for five hours at a time. He would sneak out to bars to meet old friends from the Rockaways. He felt like he was trying to break free from prison. He considered quitting, to escape the pressure. RoseEllen felt powerless and wished for her husband. Patrick had relied on Kevin. “I didn’t know anything about the Army,” she said. “I couldn’t help him.” Flaherty stepped in. “Bro, failure is not an option,” he told Patrick. “You cannot—you cannot —drop out.” He warned him that quitting would alter the trajectory of his life. Patrick rallied, though not before he missed a 9/11 anniversary ceremony because he was walking another punishment tour. This time, it was about a girl: He’d met Katie Neudeck at a party in Rockaway Beach at the end of summer break. He was supposed to report back to West Point that day, and his lateness cost him 20 hours of walking. She was motivation to graduate; so were the pictures of his father taped to his dorm-room wall, and a steel bracelet on his wrist etched with LT. KEVIN DOWDELL 9-11-01 . [ From the September 2021 issue: Jennifer Senior on what Bobby McIlvaine left behind ] James couldn’t formally enter the FDNY until he was 21, and at one point talked about joining the Marines. “No, you will not,” his mother said. Instead he enrolled at Iona. RoseEllen was alone in the house, but had two sons she still needed to get to the finish line of manhood. Patrick and James were strapping—bigger than their father, all bone and muscle and hard-charging. They had chosen dangerous futures, and there was little she could do about it. “That’s what they knew,” she said. In 2006, when James turned 21, he dropped out of his final semester at Iona to enter the FDNY academy; he then joined Ladder 174, in Flatbush. (He finished college the following year.) That same spring, Patrick graduated from West Point and prepared for deployment to Iraq. “I want to kill terrorists,” he declared to the Associated Press. By 2008, he was a platoon leader on combat patrols in Baghdad. With Patrick skirting roadside bombs and James running into fires, RoseEllen could only pray. Her faith told her that Kevin was still on watch. “I just said, in my head, He’s protecting them ,” she recalled. This is what Kevin Dowdell worked all week for: Patrick would make captain in the Army , and James would take his old man’s badge number and carry his Halligan tool. And RoseEllen— who never allowed pain, hers or theirs, to be an excuse—would see them through. While Patrick was serving abroad, James was earning a medal. At 4:30 one morning in March 2010, Ladder 174 responded to a heavy fire in a two-story building. James and another firefighter battled their way to the second floor with a fire extinguisher and, working in high heat and zero visibility, forced open the door of a rear apartment. In the smoke, James found an unconscious nine-month-old on a bed. Their team got four people out of the building alive, including the infant. James joined Rescue 2. He would be working with some of Kevin’s former colleagues, and would be expected not to drag the anchor chain, as they said in the department about slackers. In 2017, while working under Flaherty, James set the unofficial FDNY record for a rope rescue when he descended 200 feet down an unlit Con Edison shaft to help workers trapped in an underground elevator. “I was just the dope on the rope,” he said, crediting his partners who’d made the rig. Early last year, he was promoted to lieutenant—his father’s rank. He’s now studying for the captain’s exam. After Patrick left the Army as an assistant operations officer for an artillery battalion, he thought about joining the FDNY. He scored first on the entrance test, out of about 45,000 applicants, but again heard his father’s voice: I want you to do something better than me. Patrick didn’t think there was any vocation greater than firefighter, but he opted for a career in business. He works in cybersecurity in Manhattan, and his home is on the bayside of Rockaway Beach, where he can look directly at One World Trade Center and the twin light towers that shine every September 11. Each year on the anniversary, RoseEllen and her sons return to Rescue 4’s firehouse for a memorial ceremony. Firefighters gather in their dress uniforms. They bow their heads for a moment of silence in front of a plaque bearing the names of the dead. Invariably a pedestrian will pause in the firehouse driveway and say, casually, “What’s going on? Is there a parade or something?” James or Patrick will raise his head and say, “It’s September 11.” “Ohhh,” comes the reply. After the memorials, the Dowdells return to the Rockaways for a family dinner. They leave the seat at the head of the table open, with a glass of red wine in front of it. At the end of their meal, they pass around the glass, and each person tells a story about Kevin. Among those seated at the family table is a retired firefighter named Tom O’Day, whom RoseEllen began seeing in 2010 (“He understood everything,” she said). When Hurricane Sandy hit the Rockaways, RoseEllen evacuated but Tom stayed to save her possessions; he carried every memento of Kevin he could find above the flood line. In 2019, Tom and RoseEllen went to Iceland, where she buried a Mass card from Kevin’s memorial service on a remote beach, placed a rock over it, and noted the coordinates. Haruka Sakaguchi for The Atlantic James, RoseEllen, and Patrick at a 9/11 memorial in the Rockaways Five grandchildren, ages 5 through 13, are also at the family table, as are Patrick’s and James’s wives, Katie and Chrissy. They all live within walking distance of RoseEllen and the old home, where an oil portrait of Kevin hangs in the front hall. The grandchildren have been going to firehouses since they were born. As they run around, climbing and sliding down the fire pole, they talk about Grandpa Kevin as if they knew him. Recently the youngest grandchild, Carly, sat with RoseEllen, looking across Jamaica Bay. “I see Grandpa Kevin’s building,” she said. “What happened to him?” RoseEllen explained again about the bad guys who flew planes into the buildings and made them fall. [ Read: Making 9/11 relevant to young learners ] That day, reflexive acts of duty turned a terrible event into a survivable one for many people. In the aftermath, firehouses cared for the families of the fallen with something beyond duty. Beyond duty: two grieving boys hunting for their lost father and instead recovering other people’s fathers, and playing hymns for them. A firehouse full of rowdy, imperfect men finishing the job of raising them, and giving them the balm of purpose. The FDNY lost 343 men on September 11; 65 of their sons and daughters now serve in the department. Twenty-five years later, Kevin is still missing. James’s promotion to lieutenant fell on what would have been his 70th birthday. “Never Forget” is no slogan to the Dowdells. “We live it, and we live with it,” Patrick said. Living without Kevin is a form of bravery, of course—a fire all its own. Living his example is how they find their way out of the smoke. This article appears in the September 2026 print edition with the headline “Kevin Dowdell’s Boys.”

items.title: Marlon James Returns to Realism, and to Jamaica
items.description: The Jamaican writer Marlon James won international fame with A Brief History of Seven Killings , which was awarded the Booker Prize in 2015. That title misled—the book describes dozens of killings, not just seven, and it is by no means brief—but its premise delivered. The 700-page novel, his third, revisits the Jamaican election of 1976 and the assassination attempt on Bob Marley that year; the gang truce of 1978; and the violence that preceded and followed, first in Kingston, then in New York City during the 1980s and early 1990s. Lots of Americans, myself included, learned some pivotal Jamaican history and some Jamaican English and patois from its many troubled narrators. Most of those narrators seek political power, bloody revenge, wealth, or journalistic glory. The sole woman in the array—the only consistently sympathetic narrator—wants instead to disappear: “Shut everybody out. Shut everybody down. Just go.” She even pores over How to Disappear Completely and Never Be Found (it’s a real book). “Whether on a plane or in a box,” she muses, “I was going to leave this place.” James, who grew up in Kingston and now splits his time between New York City and Minneapolis, has said the same about himself: “Whether it was in a plane or in a coffin, I knew I had to get out of Jamaica.” The Disappearers , James’s new novel, shows why. Brief History studies men who want to rise, to dominate, to become stars ; this one focuses on men who try not to be seen. It’s James’s most clearly autobiographical work. Of its five main narrators, two share his age, background, and interests, and one of those misses out on the worst of Jamaica’s violence and ends up, as James has, in a stable job with an advanced degree. It’s also James’s first realist novel since Brief History— he published two long works of complex, bloody, mythological fantasy in between. This time, he writes about Jamaican men who have sex with men (only some would call themselves gay). Eight of them assemble in a Kingston home in 1988 for rehearsals of the Canadian playwright John Herbert ’s 1967 prison drama, Fortune and Men’s Eyes , under the direction of Havelock, a confident, queeny émigré who’s returned from England. Speaking in Jamaican English, as most of the characters do, he explains that it’s “a gay play about men loving and sexing and rule over other men.” None of the men who gather at the house on Lady Musgrave Road is a professional actor. All responded to flyers or heard about the play through word of mouth, and the five central narrators take turns admitting us into their minds. Eddy, a bookish university student and one of the James-like pair, combines his literary interests with a craving for porn; his passion for indie rock and X-Men comics alienates him further from his peers. Jordan, who lives in his car and hustles to survive, becomes almost a doppelgänger for Eddy: He likes comics and alternative rock too, and reads the same sort of literary books as Eddy. The group also includes a mysterious half-Chinese businessman whom Eddy can’t help finding hot; wealthy Omar, who funds the rehearsals; and three other actors. All discover, during and after rehearsals, some imaginative refuge—a space for people who, as Eddy puts it, “can’t leave but can’t stay.” They chat and flirt and grumble about what parts they’re assigned. One actor objects to playing a drag queen. Men feel they have to protect their manhood, even in this private space. Then the violence descends. A posse of men finds the house and beats almost everyone bloody or worse, using blackjacks, nunchucks, knives, fists, a crowbar, a cricket bat. James depicts the aggressors’ thoughts in a short Faulknerian fugue. At least one of the attackers is closeted: “Kill it in them, kill it in me.” Two are cops. Another’s a reggae star whose big hit “Batty Is Not Pussy” advocates killing gay men. ( Batty is Jamaican slang for “rear end,” and battyman is an insulting term for gay men.) James’s made-up star recalls the real musician Buju Banton, whose breakout track, “Boom Bye Bye”— which he’s since repudiated —also extols gay-bashing and murder. The mayhem leaves one actor dead, another blinded, and the rest hoping to rebuild, or more likely flee, their prior lives. [ From the November 2019 issue: Stephanie Burt on three books exploring the variety of transgender experiences ] The remainder of the novel follows the survivors as Jordan and Eddy attempt, separately and together, to track down those among them who have gone missing. Parts of interlocking stories unfold in the narrators’ divergent voices. Havelock writes delightfully ornate letters to his former lover in England. Jordan and Eddy relate their own travails through recorded interviews with a journalist named Petra, but also describe, in the first person, their days and years. Jordan ends up with the most eventful character arc, ultimately tracking down perpetrators too: He wants them to pay, or at least not to disappear. B rief History looks at power in a place of violence and examines what secrets it hides. Now James has written a book about people whose whole lives feel like secrets. And he has a thesis: Those who grow up learning that they are bad and do not deserve to exist—people who might get raped, maimed, or murdered for trying to be themselves—almost inevitably organize their life around attempts to disappear, escape, or else retreat to the margins, becoming (like Eddy) figures who observe others, themselves unseen, or (like Jordan) agents of vengeance who stick to the shadows. “There is a Jamaica underneath this Jamaica,” Jordan tells Eddy, whose more sheltered and luckier life means he might not know. It’s a metaphor, except when it’s not; the drag queens, trans women, and unhoused youth who live in Kingston’s gullies, below street level, have made it literal, as Eddy and Jordan, in flight from another mob later in the story, show us. James makes the gully dwellers and their fragile world a compelling side story, intent on presenting a panorama of Kingston’s gay life, from those who occupy the economic heights (also literal hills) down to “all of them queens and freaks and fishboys and battymen” who “cannot and will not pass.” The survivors of Lady Musgrave Road flee to totally closeted respectability, “a safe place filled with disappointment,” where several remain for years; or else to opportunities off the island, or religious rebirth, or a near-invisible secluded life “at the top of a mountain.” We might see the whole novel as an attempt to create a stage, a space, where gay Jamaican men can honestly and fully appear, at least in retrospect. Like Brief History , The Disappearers offers a big, modernist assemblage of contrasting styles, personas, and points of view. It, too, is a work of classic realism, touring the social layers in a changing Kingston as its characters earn and lose money, rise and fall. But unlike Brief History , which includes gay characters but mostly isn’t about them, The Disappearers also belongs with those earlier chronicles of gay America that Jordan and Eddy name-check, especially John Rechy’s The Sexual Outlaw . And so it’s full of gay sex: ecstatic, conflicted, reluctant, a desperate secret or an open secret. James acknowledges occasions of sweet, mutual, that’s-how-it-should-be sex—but those happen largely offstage. Most of the on-page couplings instead mix, alarmingly, sex with violence. Some people seek humiliation; some want to inflict it. Some get hurt by their tricks. James manages not to kink-shame anyone, but he’s less interested in kink education than in displaying a sexual world where every hookup comes with scary risks: assault and battery, for example, or public exposure, or HIV in the age before retrovirals. Living in fear of “the AIDS” entails its own “long set of disappearing acts”—not just sickness and death, but shame and denial and an inability to mourn. Those risks do not keep most of James’s survivors from pursuing, or becoming, hookups and rent boys and hate-fucks, with and without proper lube and enemas, which the novel—appropriately, even necessarily—describes: Responsible writing about anal sex has to mention those things, and James does. He wants to bring his gay men’s sex lives into the light. The men, however, keep trying to “erase themselves,” learning how to “make yourself into the kind of person nobody wants to see.” Early on, Eddy claims, “I don’t think about it a lot,” and yet he’s never unaware of being “part of an us that people just want to beat to death.” Or bury alive. The novel opens up many pleasures for literary readers, in its pacing, in its observations, and especially in the ventriloquism of Havelock’s old-school prose (he even writes one letter in the obsolescent gay slang Polari). But it’s not, mostly, a book about pleasure: These lives are often—realistically—scary or sad. We should not label them tragedies, though, because that implies a controlling divinity, or at least a fixed fate. As Havelock insists, “We need to stop calling atrocities tragic.” The Disappearers is, among other things, one novel responding to many atrocities. When you grow up surrounded by people who hate you for what you are and whom you love, it’s tough to disentangle their hate from self-hate, and either one from a wish to die. And it’s not just the cast from Lady Musgrave Road that conflates self-destruction with self-fashioning, death with destiny. So does the music of Kurt Cobain, the most important among the cultural touchstones that give Jordan and Eddy alternatives to Kingston. They listen to Nirvana, and to the rock bands that Cobain recommended—“music that people who hate me don’t like,” Jordan says—more than to “Peter Metro and Admiral Bailey” and other hitmakers from the island. [ Stephanie Burt: A strange time to be trans ] Major characters also find allies in older gay novels, like Rechy’s, and in comic books. “Come to think of it, my life is exactly like X-Men . I served a world, in this case the world of cool boys,” Eddy decides early on, “only to have those same boys abuse and brutalize me.” The heroic mutants of Marvel Comics—Nightcrawler, who looks like a devil; Storm, whom one gully queen resembles; and the rest—promise one way to survive the Kingston experience, even though, in the particular issue of X-Men that Eddy covets, the X-Men literally disappear. Renaissance writings—Shakespeare’s sonnets and King Lear , Christopher Marlowe’s Edward II —give James additional scaffolding for his stories about attachment and found family, literal torture and tortured love. The strongest subplot links the fate of Eddy’s half-Chinese crush back to the sonnets, as well as to Herbert’s play. The weakest subplot turns Jordan into an obsessive, predictable avenger, less like one of the X-Men than like a Jamaican Joker, with a twist that’s no twist at all if you’ve seen horror films. Yet up to that obvious final act, the Eddy-and-Jordan pairing works elegantly, showing two sides of the same damaged face. Still, any reader will feel for Jordan when he exclaims, late in the novel, “My ghost suffering makes me want to scream.” He means both that, compared with people dying of AIDS, he isn’t genuinely suffering (though he is), and that he feels like a disembodied outcast, a kind of ghost. The Disappearers ends up as a violence-driven protest, a scream of rage—like Nirvana’s final album—against a world that keeps trying to kill people like him and then pretends that they asked for it, or that they never existed. The novel is a superbly fashioned instrument for showing what felt wrong, what went wrong, in Jamaica in the late 1980s and ’90s, and what’s still wrong in other places, too, where people who grow up marginalized get blamed for their own persecution, or else celebrated as brave exceptions when, against the odds, they succeed. The fantastic unfairness—especially if it’s as brutal and direct as what James depicts—might make you a vanisher or an avenger (like Jordan). Or it might instead make you a chronicler (like Eddy and Petra), a maker of memorials, even a rescuer for people who want to be rescued—people who get sick of trying to disappear. And some do: Most of the survivors from Lady Musgrave Road, however wounded, find a way to forge on. Some (like Havelock) even keep trying at “building something—I don’t know, a safe place, a room of one’s own and world so you can let your hair down so to speak?” In James’s wildly patriarchal Jamaica, the struggle to live as a gay man means a struggle to become and remain some kind of man, whatever you like to do in bed. Life is, or seems to be, all about men: Women appear in the book but never narrate (as one does in Brief History ), and barely say how they feel. That’s part of the point of The Disappearers , in which the same men who persecute gay desire want women to disappear. As in any binary opposition, men learn to define themselves against their supposed other: “Nothing more shameful for a man than to be treated like a woman,” one character thinks, an idea all too familiar in the contemporary United States as well. Among the seven people who survive the Lady Musgrave Road assault, James traces some future for all but one: outside or inside Jamaica, in sham marriages that fail or desk jobs that allow them to subsist, and even in fragile, comforting, long-delayed reunions. As for that one actor who just drops out of the plot, maybe he died. After all, his “own family prefer him gone.” Or maybe that person was never a man in the first place and built a solid life elsewhere as an adult woman, her boyhood deleted for good—what trans people in earlier generations called “woodworking” (fading into the woodwork). Within The Disappearers , that’s one character’s speculation, dismissed as soon as it’s raised. But it’s also another hint of hope. And this novel, which ends in 2005, does offer hope: not just for gay Jamaican men but for trans teens, nonbinary adults, and anyone else since then who’s felt as though their society has kept asking them to hide, or lie, or die, or just go away. The Disappearers is a harrowing book, to be sure, but never nihilist, or defeatist, or cynical. Its joy in ultimate survival comes through. This article appears in the September 2026 print edition with the headline “Invisible Men.”

items.title: The Key to Understanding the Traditionalists
items.description: History Is Running Backwards In the May issue, David Brooks considered why reactionaries are taking over the world. “History Is Running Backwards” is a provocative article. But I think David Brooks errs in framing traditionalism and modernity as an either/or, when in fact they exist in a both/and context. One can be both a traditionalist and a modernist simultaneously. The key, as Brooks notes, is that “a well-adjusted life consists of daring explorations from a secure base.” Would that we all were so blessed to have that! Judy D. Cottrell Eugene, Ore. In dividing humanity into two neat psychological types—stability-seeking traditionalists and novelty-seeking progressives—Brooks misses an essential point: Psychology doesn’t exist in a vacuum; it constantly interacts with changing social factors. People who not long ago may have readily switched jobs and moved cities are now more likely to stay in place because of the scarcity of new positions and lack of affordable housing. Their psychology didn’t change—their circumstances did. Our ancestors who ventured out of Africa 1.9 million years ago were likely seeking their next meal, not the thrill of adventure. These days, people are liable to deny science and seek safety in traditional institutions because the grandest creation of modern technology—artificial intelligence—threatens everything about our way of life. Debates should focus not on psychological insecurity but on the technological, economic, and political decisions that are fostering material uncertainty and pushing people to cling to a much safer past. Allen Frances, M.D. Carmel, Calif. The fact that the traditionalists whom Brooks discusses cannot even agree on when humanity’s “fall” occurred should raise doubts about their ideology. What they are constructing is less history than creation myth: As in the story of Adam and Eve, the fall occurs when people begin thinking for themselves. History and science teach us that there never was an Eden of perfect human harmony. Civilization was built painfully, and by most measurable standards, life today is far better than it was in the past. The key to understanding the traditionalists is analyzing not the past they claim to describe but the present in which their appeals are gaining traction. Their movement has emerged as society has granted more rights to previously marginalized groups. Beneath the traditionalists’ arguments lies a recurring sentiment: My group once had the authority to define how society should function, and now it no longer does . If only people would stop questioning inherited traditions and defer once again to established authority, as defined by my group, then society could recover its lost harmony. Brooks suggests that cultivating a sense of “rootedness” might help blunt the traditionalists’ appeal. But many Americans do not see themselves reflected in what passes for American tradition. Our society does not make it easy for them to feel “rooted”—they do not see people like themselves in the literature or history they study. We need to develop broader narratives that tell the country’s whole story. That in turn can cultivate a broader sense of belonging. The humanities do need revival, as Brooks argues. But they should not be organized around a myth of decline. They should be grounded instead in the founding principles that all people are created equal and possess inalienable rights. The continuing struggle to realize those ideals could provide the shared civic story in which all Americans might find roots. Thomas M. Thurston Rosarito, Mexico Everything Is Free and Nothing Matters In the May issue, Noah Hawley described what he saw at Jeff Bezos’s Campfire retreat . F. Scott Fitzgerald once wrote, “Let me tell you about the very rich. They are different from you and me.” Ernest Hemingway, in “The Snows of Kilimanjaro,” issued a reply, writing, “Yes. They have more money.” I returned to their exchange while reading Noah Hawley’s essay about his time at Jeff Bezos’s retreat. Hawley demonstrates that Fitzgerald was indeed correct—and not merely in the way Hemingway considered. Bezos, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and their peers are so wealthy that they cannot spend all of their money in their lifetime. They really are free from consequences. Neil Ravin Hampton, N.H. Billionaires are certainly having a moment—they’re more powerful than ever. But Noah Hawley’s assertion that they are living consequence-free lives is false. After Elon Musk criticized Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” the president was clearly displeased, and a rift emerged between the two titans. But it was short-lived: Trump had the power to damage Musk’s business interests by canceling his lucrative contracts with the federal government. Political leaders still have the power to rein in billionaires—if only they’re brave enough to try. Ken Taub Saint James, N.Y. I Found It: The Best Free Restaurant Bread in America In the May issue, Caity Weaver wrote a “fun article for people to read.” When I received my print edition and saw that the cover story was about America’s “best free bread,” I was a little grumpy. The world is in chaos, democracy is withering, and this was the best The Atlantic could do? But because the story was on the cover, I sat down and read it. Turns out the answer was “Yes!” Caity Weaver’s article is an amazing novella. Her style is witty and brilliant, light and insightful. The article is a masterful piece of journalism and a true delight to read, even with its wrenching moments. Thank you for featuring something that pushed the chaos and gloom to the back of my mind for an hour. Stacey Wells Oakland, Calif. In the midst of a particularly taxing, soul-sucking, and bleak week, “I Found It: The Best Free Restaurant Bread in America” made me smile and laugh and remember that there are still lovely things to discover about the world. I’m very sorry for Weaver’s loss. I’m sure her parents would be proud that her articles have brought much joy to the world, and made a random computer programmer in Las Vegas not want to have a tantrum in the conference room. Evan Appel Las Vegas, Nev. Behind the Cover In this month’s cover story, “ Confessions of a Token Black Professor ,” Tyler Austin Harper recounts his decision to leave a tenure-track assistant professorship at Bates College, in Maine. One of the few Black faculty members, Harper came to find the college’s performative commitment to social justice suffocating, and ultimately hypocritical. On the cover, the outline of a lone figure walks away, set against the Bates seal. — Paul Spella, Senior Art Director Corrections “ Never Call Retreat ” (July) misstated the name of the labor organization that repurposed “Battle Hymn of the Republic” into “Solidarity Forever.” It was the Industrial Workers of the World, not the International Workers of the World. “ How Britain Became as Poor as Mississippi ” (July) stated that the economic gaps between London and other British cities are comparable to that between cities in West and East Germany. In fact, the economic gap between southeastern England, where London sits, and the rest of Britain is comparable to that between West and East Germany. “ So You Want a Coat of Arms ” (July) gave the incorrect impression that Kate Middleton directly received her own coat of arms. The arms were granted to her father ahead of her royal wedding. This article appears in the September 2026 print edition with the headline “The Commons.”

items.title: Le pacte de la honte et du déshonneur avec l’axe du mal
items.description: Tribune . L’Algérie nouvelle, l’Algérie des années 2020 dérange. Une partie de la droite et de l’extrême droite française a du mal à admettre l’émergence de l’Algérie. La France n’est pas seule, un autre axe du mal est clairement identifié : Les Émirats arabes unis, Maroc et Israël ou les États de l’apocalypse. Lorsqu’il s’agit de l’Algérie, le courant passe très bien entre cet axe et l'État profond français et son extrême droite. Il faut faire taire cette Algérie nouvelle, façonnée par le président Abdelmadjid Tebboune, et qui a les capacités de décider librement de son destin. Un seul mot d’ordre : l'Algérie bashing Un seul mot d’ordre : l'Algérie bashing. Pour se faire, de grandes campagnes de désinformation visant à ternir l’image de l'Algérie et de ses institutions légitimes à travers une profusion de fake news, actionnées à partir de Dubaï, Rabat, Paris, Montréal et Londres Des subversifs traîtres, qui n’ont rien d’algériens, sont recrutés, dont certains émargent officiellement à la DGSI française ! Mais peine perdue, l’Algérie est sur les rails du développement, tous les voyants sont au vert. Sale temps pour ceux qui ont pactisé avec l’axe du mal contre la grande Algérie, et qui essayent de s’accrocher vainement qui par l’invective qui par la perfidie. Face à ce torrent de haine, de tentatives de manipulation et de fake news, les Algériens se sont révélés d’efficaces contre-feux. En Algérie, ça ne tangue pas, ça ne grince pas, ça refuse de retourner à une période à jamais révolue, en Algérie, ça ne meurt pas de faim et de soif, ça ne provoque pas une émeute pour se procurer un climatiseur. C’est pourquoi ça dérange et ça hante des nuits… *Said Amer est ancien cadre de l'État Important : Les tribunes publiées sur TSA ont pour but de permettre aux lecteurs de participer au débat. Elles ne reflètent pas la position de la rédaction de notre média. L’article Le pacte de la honte et du déshonneur avec l’axe du mal est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: La FSF renforce son soutien au football régional
items.description: La Ligue régionale de football de Kédougou a clôturé, ce lundi 10 août 2026, sa saison par la grande finale régionale senior au stade Mamba Guirassy. Parrainée par le président de la Fédération sénégalaise de football (FSF), Abdoulaye Fall, la cérémonie a été marquée par la présence de Maître Papa Sidy Lo, troisième vice-président de la FSF et président du Collège des présidents de ligues régionales. Selon ce dernier, la tournée des finales régionales s’inscrit dans une volonté de renforcer l’équité territoriale et de valoriser le football amateur. Dans ce cadre, la FSF a accordé à chaque ligue une subvention de 6 millions de francs CFA pour l’organisation de sa finale. L’enveloppe couvre notamment les frais d’organisation et les récompenses des champions et vice-champions. La Fédération a également prévu des trophées pour les champions, les équipes fair-play, ainsi que pour les meilleurs joueurs, buteurs et gardiens. Des kits pédagogiques tactico-techniques ont aussi été remis aux équipes finalistes afin d’améliorer leur préparation et de renforcer la formation à la base. Le président de la Ligue régionale, Sadio Cissokho, s’est réjoui de la mobilisation et surtout de la discipline des équipes, estimant que le niveau de jeu présenté est digne du championnat national. Il a toutefois déploré le déficit d’infrastructures sportives et les difficultés de mobilité qui pénalisent les clubs d’une région vaste et éloignée. Il salue les projets de construction du stade régional et des stades départementaux, tout en appelant les entreprises locales à davantage soutenir les clubs par le sponsoring. Sadio Cissokho invite également les collectivités territoriales à réserver des espaces dédiés au sport dans les opérations d’aménagement urbain, afin de permettre aux jeunes de disposer de terrains de proximité.. Amadou DIOP (Correspondant)

items.title: Covid-19 : une étude controversée sur la surmortalité retirée pour « désinformation »
items.description: Une étude publiée en 2024 sur la surmortalité après le pic de la pandémie de Covid-19 vient d’être retirée de la revue BMJ Public Health. L’éditeur estime qu’elle pouvait contribuer à une interprétation trompeuse des causes de cette surmortalité. Le BMJ Group, qui édite la revue, a annoncé le retrait de cette étude après plusieurs critiques concernant sa méthodologie et ses conclusions. Le travail avait notamment été largement relayé par des publications vaccinosceptiques, qui affirmaient qu’il établissait un lien entre la vaccination contre le Covid-19 et la surmortalité. Or, l’étude ne démontrait pas de lien de causalité entre les vaccins et les décès supplémentaires. Ses auteurs s’interrogeaient toutefois sur la persistance de la surmortalité malgré les mesures prises pendant la pandémie, notamment les confinements et la vaccination. Cette formulation avait suscité de nombreuses critiques et conduit le BMJ Group à ouvrir une enquête. Le Centre Princess Maxima, auquel étaient affiliés trois des quatre auteurs, avait également lancé un examen. L’éditeur estime finalement que l’étude véhiculait « de la désinformation sur les causes possibles de la surmortalité » et reposait sur une quantité limitée de travail original. Le retrait est soutenu par deux des quatre auteurs ainsi que par le Centre Princess Máxima. Cette décision constitue un désaveu majeur de la publication, sans pour autant remettre en cause l’ensemble des recherches scientifiques consacrées à la surmortalité ou aux vaccins contre le Covid-19. The post Covid-19 : une étude controversée sur la surmortalité retirée pour « désinformation » appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Touba Darou Marnane : Trois ans de pénurie d’eau, les populations montent au créneau
items.description: Confrontées à un manque d’eau depuis plusieurs années, les populations de Touba Darou Marnane sont sorties de leur mutisme. Face à la presse, lundi 10 août 2026, elles ont interpellé les autorités administratives et religieuses sur une situation qui, selon elles, perdure depuis plus de trois ans. Femmes, hommes, jeunes et adultes ont investi les rues de la localité, munis de bouteilles et de bassines, pour réclamer l’accès à l’eau. Selon les manifestants, cette pénurie est devenue une difficulté quotidienne, obligeant les habitants à parcourir plusieurs quartiers à la recherche du liquide précieux. « Nous sommes contraints de sortir manifester les difficultés auxquelles nous faisons face », a expliqué Médoune Sèye. D’après lui, le problème d’approvisionnement en eau reste entier depuis plus de trois ans. Une situation qui, à l’en croire, n’a pas reçu jusqu’ici la réponse attendue de la part des autorités. « Ça a vraiment duré, au moment où nos autorités semblaient ne pas être au courant. Nous sollicitons de l’aide », a-t-il lancé. Médoune Sèye dénonce particulièrement les difficultés rencontrées par les femmes. Selon lui, ces dernières sont obligées de faire le tour des quartiers voisins pour trouver quelques bouteilles d’eau nécessaires aux besoins de leurs familles. Une corvée devenue, dit-il, une préoccupation quotidienne pour de nombreux ménages. La situation se serait davantage aggravée lors du Grand Magal de Touba. Avec l’affluence exceptionnelle enregistrée pendant cet événement religieux, les besoins en eau ont considérablement augmenté. Médoune Sèye affirme que les habitants étaient alors contraints de recourir aux camions-citernes, avec des dépenses pouvant atteindre 50 000 francs CFA pour un seul camion. Des propos confirmés par Awa Athie. La jeune femme souligne que cette pénurie a également eu des conséquences sur l’accueil des pèlerins venus passer le Magal dans la localité. « Certains de nos hôtes préfèrent aller chercher un autre lieu d’hébergement à cause du problème de l’eau », déplore-t-elle. Awa Athie avance par ailleurs une explication à cette situation. Elle estime que les travaux d’assainissement réalisés dans le quartier il y a quelques années auraient endommagé le réseau hydraulique destiné à l’approvisionnement de la zone. Elle demande ainsi aux autorités de se pencher sérieusement sur cette question afin de trouver une solution durable à un problème qui, selon elle, n’a que trop duré. Non loin d'elle, Astou Diagne insiste sur le poids de cette pénurie dans le quotidien des habitants. « Toutes nos préoccupations sont tournées vers la recherche de l’eau », dénonce-t-elle. Pour elle, trouver de l’eau est devenu un véritable parcours du combattant, au détriment des autres activités des populations. Face à cette situation, les habitants de Touba Darou Marnane lancent un appel aux autorités administratives, mais aussi aux autorités religieuses. Ils souhaitent une intervention rapide pour mettre fin à cette pénurie qui affecte leur quotidien depuis plusieurs années. « Nous ne voulons que de l’eau. Nous sollicitons l’aide du khalife général des mourides », conclut Astou Diagne. Birane DIOP (Correspondant)

items.title: Nord Foire : sept personnes déférées pour proxénétisme et prostitution clandestine
items.description: Le Commissariat spécial du Tourisme a déféré au parquet, le 10 août 2026, sept personnes interpellées dans le cadre d’une affaire présumée de prostitution clandestine, de proxénétisme et de mise en danger de la vie d’autrui. L’affaire a débuté à la suite d’un renseignement faisant état des activités d’un réseau de proxénétisme et de prostitution clandestine qui aurait établi ses quartiers dans un restaurant-bar et une auberge situés à Nord Foire. Les informations recueillies par les enquêteurs faisaient également état de soupçons de blanchiment de capitaux et de la présence présumée de prostituées étrangères ainsi que de mineures. À la suite de ces signalements, les éléments du Commissariat spécial du Tourisme ont effectué une descente dans l’établissement. Cinq femmes ont alors été interpellées. Il s’agit d’une Sénégalaise et de quatre Nigérianes, poursuivies notamment pour non-inscription au fichier sanitaire et social (NIFSS) et mise en danger de la vie d’autrui. Selon les premiers éléments de l’enquête, les mises en cause exerçaient clandestinement la prostitution au sein de l’établissement. Les investigations ont par ailleurs conduit à l’interpellation de la réceptionniste et du gérant, soupçonnés d’avoir facilité cette activité et d’en avoir tiré profit. Ils sont poursuivis pour proxénétisme. Au terme de la procédure, les sept mis en cause ont été déférés au parquet. L’enquête devra notamment permettre de déterminer l’étendue du réseau, les responsabilités de chacun et de vérifier les autres faits signalés, notamment les soupçons de blanchiment de capitaux et la présence éventuelle de mineures. A.N

items.title: Vacances actives à Ouagadougou : Sur les trottoirs, des enfants vendent leurs rêves au rythme des feux rouges
items.description: À Ouagadougou, les vacances scolaires ne riment pas avec repos pour tous. Chaque jour, aux carrefours de la capitale, des jeunes garçons arpentent les trottoirs et s'approchent des véhicules à l'arrêt pour vendre divers articles. Derrière leurs sourires se cachent des sacrifices précoces, des responsabilités lourdes et des rêves d'un avenir meilleur. Constat le vendredi 31 juillet 2026 sur les activités de ces vacanciers. Alors que la majorité des élèves profitent de la trêve estivale pour se détendre, d'autres ont fait un choix différent : celui du travail. Dès les premières heures de la matinée, plusieurs carrefours de la capitale se transforment en espaces de commerce improvisés. Ces jeunes vendeurs attendent patiemment que le feu passe au rouge pour entrer en action. Des jeunes qui patientent que le feu passe au rouge pour espérer vendre Lotus, torchons, pare-soleil, bouteilles d'eau, jouets ou accessoires automobiles à la main, ils disposent de quelques secondes pour convaincre les automobilistes. Chaque arrêt est une course contre la montre. Chaque vente représente un pas supplémentaire vers leurs objectifs. Ces activités révèlent pourtant des histoires de vie marquées par une maturité étonnante. Pour certains, l'argent gagné permettra d'acheter les fournitures scolaires, de payer les frais de scolarité ou de renouveler l'uniforme pour la prochaine rentrée. Pour d'autres, il s'agit surtout d'alléger les charges de leurs parents ou de contribuer aux dépenses familiales dans un contexte économique difficile. C'est le choix qu'a fait Mouslim Belem, admis en classe de 5e. Depuis les vacances de l'année dernière, il consacre une partie de son temps libre à la vente au bord de la route. « Je vends pour venir en aide à mes parents. L'argent me sert à acheter mon sac, mes cahiers et à participer aux frais de scolarité. Nous sommes nombreux dans la famille, donc ce n'est pas facile pour eux de payer l'école de chacun. Si j'arrive à apporter 5 000 ou 10 000 F CFA, cela les aide énormément. Depuis que j'ai commencé, j'ai compris les sacrifices qu'ils font chaque jour pour prendre soin de nous. J'invite mes camarades à travailler pendant les vacances. La vie n'est pas facile et il ne faut pas passer tout son temps à jouer au football », confie-t-il. Des vendeurs ambulants… À son jeune âge, Mouslim dit avoir découvert une réalité qu'il ne soupçonnait pas. Il s'agit de la difficulté de gagner de l'argent. Une expérience qui a renforcé son respect envers ses parents et développé en lui le goût de l'effort. Malgré leur âge, ces vendeurs affrontent quotidiennement la chaleur, la poussière, les gaz d'échappement et les dangers de la circulation. Des risques qu'ils acceptent de courir dans l'espoir d'offrir un meilleur avenir à leur famille. Élève en classe de CM1, Wilfrid Nana fait partie de ces enfants déterminés. « Je fais ce travail pour aider mes parents, pour qu'ils puissent compléter ce que je gagne et payer ma scolarité. J'ai commencé cette année. Plus tard, je veux ouvrir une boutique et devenir un grand commerçant. J'encourage tous les enfants à aimer le travail », explique-t-il. Malgré tout, Wilfrid garde le sourire et poursuit son activité avec courage, convaincu que chaque article vendu le rapproche un peu plus de ses objectifs. Pour Hamza Temsabedo, qui passe en classe de CM2, les vacances sont avant tout une période de solidarité familiale. « Je viens aider mon grand frère à vendre. Pour chaque sachet de lotus vendu, je gagne 125 FCFA. Je garde cet argent jusqu'à la rentrée pour payer ma scolarité et aider mes parents. J'encourage aussi mes camarades à travailler pour soutenir leurs familles et obtenir la bénédiction de leurs parents », raconte-t-il. Plus âgé, Idrissa Bougma assume pleinement les risques liés à cette activité. « Je fais ce travail pour prendre soin de ma famille. Certains jours, je peux gagner 5 000 FCFA ou plus. Travailler au milieu de la route est dangereux, mais quand c'est pour aider les siens, on accepte ce sacrifice. Je demande aux jeunes de chercher une activité au lieu de dire qu'il n'y a pas de travail. Même un petit boulot peut permettre de subvenir aux besoins de sa famille. Si on ne fait aucun effort, personne ne viendra le faire à notre place », témoigne-t-il. À travers leur engagement, ces enfants démontrent qu'il existe une autre voie que l'oisiveté ou la délinquance. Ils choisissent l'effort, la persévérance et le travail honnête, malgré les difficultés et les risques auxquels ils sont confrontés chaque jour. items.title: JI sends Rs1bn defamation notice to ex-FBR chief Shabbar Zaidi
items.description: Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) has sent a legal notice to former Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) chairman Shabbar Zaidi and sought Rs1 billion in damages over allegations that the party received money to suppress public protests, according to a statement by the JI. The statement said the legal notice was sent on July 27 through Advocate Tahir Iqbal Malik on the directives of the party’s Karachi General Secretary Taufiquddin Siddiqui. When Dawn contacted Zaidi for his comment on Tuesday, the former FBR chief said he had forwarded the notice to his lawyer for legal advice. The JI’s statement, citing the party’s notice, said Zaidi made serious allegations against the party during a podcast interview and subsequently in statements circulated on YouTube, Facebook, X, TikTok, WhatsApp and other social media platforms. The notice alleged that the former FBR chairman described the party as the “establishment’s firewall” for “diluting” public issues and protests. In the notice, the statement said, JI’s lawyer contended that Zaidi’s statements amounted to “serious allegations against the party, including secret funding, bribery, corruption, political deception, betrayal of public interests, and alleged collusion with state elements”. Through the notice, the JI demanded that Zaidi provides complete evidence in support of his claim, including the identity of person who allegedly made the payment; the name of person who received the money; the amount paid; the date, time and place of the payment; the method of payment; the relevant bank account or financial document; details of the alleged protest or public issue; witnesses to the transaction, documents and recordings; and the source on the basis of which the allegation was made, the statement said.

items.title: Niger : 22 morts, dont 17 militaires, dans une collision entre deux bus sur l’axe Maradi-Madaoua
items.description: Une collision entre deux autobus de transport de voyageurs a fait 22 morts et 37 blesses vendredi 7 août 2026 sur l'axe Maradi-Madaoua, au Niger. Les deux vehicules appartenaient aux compagnies SONITRAV et STM. Parmi les personnes decedees figurent 17 militaires, selon le ministere nigerien des Transports. L'accident s'est produit a hauteur de Doukou Doukou, a environ 55 kilometres de Madaoua. Dans sa premiere depeche publiee le 8 août, l'Agence Nigerienne de Presse (ANP) faisait etat d'un bilan provisoire de 21 morts et 37 blesses. Deux jours plus tard, le 10 août, le bilan actualise est passe a de 22 deces et 37 blesses. Deux bus violemment entres en collision Selon les premiers elements communiques par la gendarmerie, l'accident a implique un bus de la compagnie SONITRAV venant de Maradi, qui transportait notamment des militaires, et un vehicule de la compagnie STM venant de Madaoua. Les deux autobus se sont violemment heurtes avant de quitter leur trajectoire. Le commandant de bataillon de la gendarmerie de Madaoua, cite par l'ANP, a indique que le bus de la STM avait poursuivi sa course sur environ 170 metres, tandis que celui de SONITRAV avait parcouru environ 96 metres apres le choc. L'un des conducteurs etait decede lors de la collision, selon la meme source. Les 37 blesses ont ete pris en charge par les services sanitaires. Dans le premier bilan diffuse le 8 août, la gendarmerie indiquait que les victimes decedees avaient ete transportees a l'hopital de district de Madaoua et que les blesses avaient ete evacues vers Madaoua et Maradi, dont neuf vers Maradi. Dix-sept militaires parmi les victimes Un bilan communique par le ministere nigerien des Transports et relaye a etabli que 17 des 22 personnes decedees etaient des militaires. Le 8 août, avant la publication de ce bilan actualise, les autorites et responsables des Forces de defense et de securite de la region de Maradi avaient rendu un dernier hommage a 16 membres des Forces de defense et de securite dont les corps se trouvaient a la morgue de Maradi. Une priere mortuaire avait ete organisee avant leur inhumation au cimetiere musulman de la ville. Une enquete ouverte sur les causes de l'accident Les circonstances precises ayant conduit a la collision n'ont pas encore ete etablies publiquement. Des le 8 août, la gendarmerie avait annonce l'ouverture d'une enquete destinee a determiner les causes de l'accident. Le 10 août, le ministre des Transports et de l'Aviation civile, le colonel-major Abdouramane Amadou, a convoque les responsables des compagnies STM et SONITRAV pour une reunion consacree au drame. Selon le communique rapporte par l' ANP , les representants des deux entreprises ont ete entendus sur leurs responsabilites respectives et ont recu des instructions pour corriger les manquements constates. Le ministre a estime que le comportement humain demeure un facteur fondamental dans ce type d'accident et a denonce les comportements imprudents de certains conducteurs ainsi que l'indulgence dont leurs employeurs peuvent faire preuve. Cette appreciation generale des autorites ne constitue toutefois pas, a ce stade, une conclusion de l'enquete sur la responsabilite precise de l'une ou l'autre compagnie dans l'accident du 7 août. Des sanctions envisagees contre la compagnie qui serait reconnue responsable Le ministere des Transports a annonce que des sanctions seraient prises contre la societe dont la responsabilite serait etablie. Selon la gravite des manquements retenus, les mesures prevues peuvent aller de l'avertissement a la suspension, voire au retrait de l'agrement d'exploitation, independamment d'eventuelles poursuites judiciaires decidees par les autorites competentes. La reunion du 10 août s'est tenue en presence de responsables du ministere des Transports et de l'Aviation civile, de l'Agence Nigerienne de Securite Routiere (ANISER) et de la Gendarmerie nationale. Un drame dans un contexte de forte mortalite routiere Cette collision intervient alors que les autorites nigeriennes ont declare 2026 « Annee de la Discipline Routiere », une initiative annoncee en avril par le ministere des Transports et de l'Aviation civile afin de renforcer la securite sur les routes. Les statistiques officielles illustrent l'ampleur du probleme. Selon des donnees communiquees en avril 2026 et reprises par l'ANP, 7 116 accidents corporels ont ete enregistres au Niger en 2025, faisant 1 245 morts et 4 439 blesses graves.

items.title: Bintou Signate et Mouhamadou Nazirou Diankha veulent révolutionner la seconde main au Sénégal
items.description: Tekkofi entend bousculer les habitudes de vente entre particuliers. Avec ses annonces vocales, l’absence de commission et sa messagerie intégrée, elle veut offrir une alternative aux échanges dispersés sur les réseaux sociaux, tout en misant sur l’économie circulaire et les usages locaux. Acheter un meuble, un vêtement ou encore un appareil électronique répond à un besoin. Mais dans certains cas, ils finissent souvent au placard ou sur le toit d’une terrasse. C’est ce constat qui a poussé Bintou Signate et Mouhamadou Nazirou Diankha a créé « Tekkofi ». Lancée le 11 juillet 2026, cette plateforme qui compte plus d’une centaine d'utilisateurs vise à donner une seconde vie à un objet et aide à trouver facilement ce dont on a besoin. « Un particulier peut vendre un objet pour générer un revenu complémentaire ou choisir de le donner. Un professionnel peut présenter son activité, développer sa visibilité et toucher de nouveaux clients. Le tout dans un environnement simple, sécurisé et pensé pour les habitudes des utilisateurs sénégalais. Avec Mouhamadou Nazirou Diankha, nous avons voulu construire une plateforme qui réponde à tous ces besoins », a expliqué Bintou Signate.À l’en croire, Tekkofi n'est pas seulement une plateforme de petites annonces. C'est une façon de repenser notre manière de consommer, de vendre, de partager et de créer de la valeur à partir de ce que nous possédons déjà. Le choix du nom Tekkofi est le reflet meme de l'identité que les deux concepteurs veulent donner à la plateforme.« En wolof, il signifie « pose-le ici ». Cette expression traduit parfaitement l'idée de la plateforme : un espace où chacun peut déposer quelque chose, un objet à vendre ou à donner, un produit à présenter, un service à proposer, ou simplement une opportunité à partager. C'est un lieu d'échange où ce qui est déposé peut trouver une nouvelle valeur auprès d'une autre personne », a expliqué Bintou. Cette dernière précise également que le choix du nom est aussi une référence sonore à « take coffee » en anglais. « Le café évoque un moment simple et convivial : un espace où les personnes se rencontrent, échangent et créent des liens. Cette dimension représente notre ambition de faire de Tekkofi plus qu'un outil numérique : un espace de connexion entre les personnes avec des ambitions internationales », a-t-elle relevé. Ni WhatsApp encore moins Tiktok Tekkofi n’est pas Facebook encore moins WhatsApp. C’est ce que souligne Bintou Signate.« Ces outils ont permis à de nombreux vendeurs, entrepreneurs et particuliers de commencer à présenter leurs produits sur Internet. Cependant, ils fonctionnent principalement à partir d'un réseau existant », nuance Bintou. Sur WhatsApp Business, poursuit-elle, pour découvrir les produits d'un vendeur, il faut généralement déjà connaître son numéro ou l'avoir déjà dans ses contacts. Cela limite naturellement la visibilité des vendeurs : un commerçant peut avoir de bons produits, mais rester invisible auprès de personnes qui ne connaissent pas encore son activité ou l'avoir déjà dans ses contacts. « Avec Tekkofi, nous avons voulu inverser cette logique. La plateforme permet aux utilisateurs de découvrir des produits et des services au-delà de leur propre réseau. Un acheteur peut rechercher un article, comparer plusieurs offres et trouver un vendeur sans avoir besoin de connaître son numéro de téléphone au préalable », renseigne la cofondatrice de Tekkofi. Tekkofi possède également une fonctionnalité d’annonce vocale. Cela rend la plateforme accessible à ceux qui sont peu à l'aise avec l'écrit.« En sus de cela, il y a le 0% de commission, qui garantit aux vendeurs de garder l'intégralité de leurs gains ainsi que la messagerie interne, qui protège la vie privée des utilisateurs. C'est une plateforme pensée par des Sénégalais, pour les réalités sénégalaises », insiste-t-elle. Cette dernière souligne aussi que la plateforme a été pensé autour des réalités de la seconde main.« Beaucoup de personnes ont aujourd'hui des objets qu'elles n'utilisent plus et qui pourraient être utiles à d'autres. La plateforme leur permet de vendre, mais aussi de donner une seconde vie à ces objets », explique-t-elle. Seconde main, seconde vie « Nous accumulons des objets, des vêtements, des appareils électroniques ou du mobilier qui finissent souvent oubliés dans un placard ou un garage. Pourtant, ils ont encore de la valeur et pourraient être utiles à d'autres. Dans le même temps, de nombreuses personnes recherchent des alternatives plus abordables pour s'équiper, tandis que d'autres souhaitent consommer de manière plus responsable en privilégiant la seconde main », constate Bintou. À l’en croire, c’est justement ces observations qui ont motivé la création de Tekkofi. « Notre ambition n'est pas de remplacer les outils que les Sénégalais utilisent déjà, mais de proposer un espace complémentaire, plus structuré et pensé pour leurs besoins : rechercher, comparer, acheter, vendre, donner et développer une activité », a fait savoir Bintou. Au-delà de l'aspect économique, enchaine-t-elle, l’objectif est pour eux de contribuer à faire évoluer notre manière de consommer en encourageant une logique d'économie circulaire.« Aujourd’hui, avec Tekkofi, nous voulons l donner une seconde vie aux objets en facilitant leur circulation entre les personnes », milite-t-elle. Bintou Signate explique que chaque article vendu ou donné sur la plateforme représente un objet qui continue d'être utile, et potentiellement un achat neuf évité. Cela permet de limiter le gaspillage, de prolonger la durée de vie des produits et de réduire l'impact environnemental lié à la production de nouveaux biens. « Cette approche rejoint plusieurs Objectifs de Développement Durable des Nations Unies, notamment l'ODD 12 sur la consommation et la production responsables, qui encourage une utilisation plus durable des ressources et la réduction des déchets. Elle s'inscrit également dans une réflexion plus large autour de l'ODD 11 sur les villes et communautés durables, en favorisant des modes de consommation plus responsables au sein des territoires », soutient Bintou. La cofondatrice de Tekkofi rappelle aussi que dans le contexte sénégalais, où les pratiques de réutilisation, de partage et de transmission existent déjà depuis longtemps, leur ambition est d'utiliser le numérique pour renforcer ces dynamiques et leur donner une nouvelle échelle. « Nous ne prétendons pas résoudre à nous seuls les enjeux environnementaux, mais nous voulons contribuer à un changement progressif des habitudes : acheter autrement, vendre ce qui n'est plus utilisé, donner plutôt que jeter, et considérer chaque objet comme une ressource qui peut encore créer de la valeur », ambitionne-t-elle. « Nous ne comptons pas nous arrêter en si bon chemin. Notre ambition est de construire une plateforme qui accompagne l'utilisateur tout au long de son parcours : trouver un produit, échanger avec un vendeur, finaliser un achat et, à terme, faciliter davantage la transaction », annonce Bintou Signate. Mais la jeune femme souligne que leur ambition dépasse nos frontières.« Dans cinq ans, nous voulons que Tekkofi soit une plateforme africaine de référence pour la vente entre particuliers et professionnels, reconnue pour son accessibilité et sa proximité avec les usages réels des populations. Une technologie qui se sera adaptée à ses utilisateurs, et non l'inverse », souhaite-t-elle. Des ambitions ancrées entre ouverture et enracinement. Arame NDIAYE
